name: A01:2025 Broken Access Control
description: Users act outside their intended permissions; includes server-side request forgery.
key_questions: Where is each authorization decision enforced, and is it on the server?|Can a user reach another user's records by changing an id in a request?|Which endpoints or admin functions have no role check?|Can the server be made to fetch a URL an attacker chooses?|Is access denied by default?

name: A02:2025 Security Misconfiguration
description: Insecure defaults, unneeded features, verbose errors or missing hardening in any layer.
key_questions: Which default accounts, ports, sample apps or debug features are still enabled?|How is configuration kept consistent across environments, and who can change it?|Are security headers and cloud storage permissions set on purpose?|Do error responses reveal stack traces or versions?

name: A03:2025 Software Supply Chain Failures
description: Compromise through dependencies, build systems or distribution channels.
key_questions: Is there an inventory of every direct and transitive dependency with its version?|How are new dependencies vetted and updates applied?|Who can change the build pipeline, and are its outputs signed?|What happens when a dependency is reported vulnerable?|Are packages and images pulled only from trusted sources?

name: A04:2025 Cryptographic Failures
description: Sensitive data exposed through missing, weak or misused cryptography.
key_questions: Which data is sensitive, and is it encrypted in transit and at rest?|Which algorithms, key lengths and modes are in use?|Where are keys stored, who can read them, and how are they rotated?|How are passwords hashed?|Do tokens and secrets come from a cryptographically secure random source?

name: A05:2025 Injection
description: Untrusted input interpreted as code or commands: SQL, NoSQL, OS commands, LDAP, cross-site scripting.
key_questions: Where does untrusted input reach an interpreter, query or shell?|Are queries parameterized everywhere, including reports and admin tools?|Is output encoded for the context it lands in?|Is input validated on the server against what is allowed?|Does any prompt or template mix user input with instructions?

name: A06:2025 Insecure Design
description: Controls missing or ineffective at the design level, which no implementation can fix.
key_questions: Which threats were considered when the design was made?|Which business flows can be abused by repetition, automation or steps out of order?|Where are rate limits and resource quotas?|Are tenants and trust levels separated by design?|Which security requirements have tests?

name: A07:2025 Authentication Failures
description: Weaknesses in confirming identity and managing sessions.
key_questions: Where is multi-factor authentication offered or required?|What stops credential stuffing and brute force?|How are sessions created, expired and invalidated on logout or password change?|How does account recovery prove identity?|Are default and known-breached passwords rejected?

name: A08:2025 Software or Data Integrity Failures
description: Code or data trusted without checking it was not altered: unsigned updates, insecure deserialization, untrusted pipeline inputs.
key_questions: How are updates and plugins verified before they run?|Is untrusted data ever deserialized into objects?|Which data crossing a trust boundary is checked for tampering?|Can a pull request or other outside input change what the pipeline deploys?

name: A09:2025 Security Logging & Alerting Failures
description: Attacks go unnoticed because events are not logged, watched or alerted on.
key_questions: Which security events are logged: logins, access failures, high-value transactions?|Can logs be altered, and do they contain sensitive data?|Who receives an alert, and how fast?|Has the incident response plan been exercised?|Could an attacker's actions be reconstructed from the logs?

name: A10:2025 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions
description: Errors, edge cases and abnormal states handled so the system fails open, leaks data or loses consistency.
key_questions: When a dependency times out or errors, does the system fail closed?|Can a partial failure leave a transaction half done?|What does an unhandled exception show the user?|How does the system behave under resource exhaustion or malformed input?|Are error paths tested?

name: Spoofing
description: Pretending to be another user, service or component; threatens authentication.
key_questions: How does each component prove its identity to the others?|Which entry points accept a claimed identity without verifying it?|How are service credentials and tokens issued, stored and revoked?|Can a captured token be replayed?

name: Tampering
description: Changing data or code without authorization; threatens integrity.
key_questions: Which data in transit or at rest could be changed by someone who should not?|Where is integrity checked: signatures, hashes, database constraints?|Can a client alter values the server trusts, such as prices or roles?|Who can change code, configuration or the build?

name: Repudiation
description: Denying an action when the system cannot prove who did it; threatens non-repudiation.
key_questions: Which actions could a user deny that the system must be able to prove?|Does the audit trail record who, what and when for those actions?|Are audit logs protected from the people they record?|Do timestamps come from a trusted clock?

name: Information Disclosure
description: Exposing data to someone not allowed to see it; threatens confidentiality.
key_questions: Which data would cause harm if exposed, and who may see it?|Where could it leak: logs, errors, caches, backups, side channels?|Do responses and stores hold only the data they need?|What crosses a trust boundary unencrypted?

name: Denial of Service
description: Making the system unavailable or degraded for legitimate users; threatens availability.
key_questions: Which resources can an unauthenticated caller exhaust?|Where are rate limits, timeouts and quotas?|Which single component's failure takes the system down?|What is the most expensive request an attacker can send?

name: Elevation of Privilege
description: Gaining capabilities beyond those granted; threatens authorization.
key_questions: Where does a lower-trust caller reach higher-trust code?|Can a normal user reach admin functions or another tenant's data?|Does each component run with only the privileges it needs?|Which inputs could lead to code execution?
